title: Import and Export Basics
summary: Learn how international trade works: trade agreements including AfCFTA, market research and HS codes, Incoterms and landed-cost calculations, payment methods and currency risk, documents and customs, and managing trade risks.
audience: Traders, entrepreneurs, procurement staff and business students interested in cross-border trade

body.p: Countries trade because they have different resources, skills and costs. Exporting lets businesses reach larger markets and earn foreign currency; importing gives access to goods, machinery and inputs that are unavailable or more expensive locally. Africa's exports have long been dominated by raw commodities, and adding value through processing before export is a major opportunity.

list: The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) aims to remove most tariffs between African countries and simplify trade.
Regional communities such as ECOWAS, the EAC, SADC and COMESA have their own trade arrangements.
Preference schemes, such as the United States' AGOA, have offered duty-free access for many African products, subject to renewal and conditions.
Rules of origin decide whether a product qualifies for lower duties: usually it must be made or substantially processed in the member country.

body.p: Every trader should also know their country's export promotion agency, customs authority and standards bodies; they provide market information, documentation and support.

body.tip: Start by exporting to a nearby regional market; shorter distances, familiar customs and trade agreements make the first shipment easier.

body.p: Research before exporting: demand, competition, prices, regulations, standards, labelling rules, cultural preferences and logistics costs. Trade statistics show which countries already import your product and in what quantities.

Every traded product has a Harmonized System (HS) code, an internationally agreed number used for customs, tariffs and statistics. The first six digits are the same worldwide; countries add further digits. The correct code decides the duty rate and any restrictions, so classify carefully and ask customs for a ruling if unsure.

list: Food and agricultural products may need sanitary and phytosanitary certificates.
Many markets set maximum pesticide residues and strict labelling rules.
Some goods need import or export permits (medicines, chemicals, endangered species).
Product standards and certification (quality, safety, electrical) may be compulsory.

body.tip: Ask potential buyers which certificates and standards they require before you produce the goods, not after.

body.p: Incoterms define who pays for and bears the risk of each stage of transport. Common terms: EXW (buyer collects at the seller's premises), FCA, FOB (seller loads goods onto the vessel), CIF (seller pays freight and insurance to the destination port, but risk passes at loading), DAP and DDP (seller delivers to the buyer's place, with duties paid under DDP).

An importer buys 1000 units FOB for $10 000. Freight costs $1200 and insurance $150, so the CIF value is $11 350. If import duty is 20% of CIF, duty is $2270. If VAT of 15% is charged on CIF plus duty ($13 620), VAT is about $2043. The landed cost is about $15 663, or $15.66 per unit, before clearing fees, port charges and local transport. (Duty and VAT bases differ by country; check local rules. Registered businesses can often reclaim import VAT.)

Exporters build prices upwards from their costs: production, packaging, inland transport, export documents and any costs their chosen Incoterm includes, then add margin. A product costing $25 to make and deliver FOB, priced with a 30% markup, sells for $32.50, or $32 500 for 1000 units.

body.tip: Always calculate the full landed cost before agreeing a price; duties and fees can turn a profitable deal into a loss.

body.p: International buyers and sellers rarely know each other well, so payment methods balance risk between them.

list: Cash in advance: safest for the exporter, riskiest for the importer.
Letter of credit: the buyer's bank promises to pay once the exporter presents documents that exactly match the terms; secure but more costly and paperwork-heavy.
Documentary collection: banks exchange shipping documents for payment or a signed promise to pay; cheaper but less secure than a letter of credit.
Open account: goods are shipped and paid for later; common between trusted partners, riskiest for the exporter. Trade credit insurance can reduce the risk.

body.p: If a South African importer owes $10 000 in 90 days, at R18 per dollar that is R180 000; if the rand weakens to R19, the bill becomes R190 000, R10 000 more. Forward contracts with a bank fix the rate in advance, removing this uncertainty at a small cost. Invoicing in your own currency moves the risk to the other party.

body.tip: Never ship on open account to a new buyer you have not checked; start with secure terms and relax them as trust grows.

body.p: Shipments move only when the paperwork is right. Errors cause delays, storage charges, fines and even seizure.

list: Commercial invoice: describes the goods, value, buyer, seller and Incoterm.
Packing list: contents, weights and dimensions of each package.
Bill of lading (sea) or air waybill (air): the transport contract and receipt; an original bill of lading can also be a title document.
Certificate of origin: proves where goods were made, needed for preferential duties.
Customs declaration, permits, inspection and health certificates where required.
Insurance certificate.

body.p: Licensed customs clearing agents and freight forwarders prepare declarations, arrange transport and handle port procedures. Choose experienced, reputable agents, give them accurate information, and check their declarations; the importer or exporter remains responsible for what is declared.

body.tip: Make sure the description, quantities and values match exactly across every document; inconsistencies are a leading cause of delays.

body.p: International trade carries risks beyond payment and currency: goods can be lost or damaged, buyers may reject goods, regulations change and fraudsters target traders.

list: Insure cargo for its full value plus a margin.
Check new partners: company registration, references, trade fair contacts and bank checks.
Use written contracts covering specifications, inspection, Incoterms, payment, delivery dates and dispute resolution.
Watch for fraud: changed bank details in emails, too-good-to-be-true orders and fake documents. Confirm payment details by phone using a known number.
Comply with sanctions, anti-money-laundering and anti-corruption laws; never pay bribes to speed up clearance.
Keep records for the period customs and tax laws require.

body.p: Start with one product and one market, learn, then expand. Use export promotion agencies, trade fairs and online business-to-business platforms to find buyers, and build reputation through consistent quality and reliable delivery.

body.tip: If a supplier or buyer emails new bank details, call them on a number you already have before paying anything.

quiz.q: What is the main aim of the AfCFTA?
options: Reducing tariffs and simplifying trade between African countries

quiz.q: What do rules of origin decide?
options: Whether goods qualify for preferential duty rates

quiz.q: What is an HS code used for?
options: Classifying products for customs and tariffs
